RHYTHM DISORDERS AND ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY
CLINICAL CASE
Concealed Wenckebach Phenomenon
in Left Bundle Branch Associated
With Chest Pain
Marco Marino, MD,a Gianluca Massaro, MD,a Vincenzo Carbone, MD,b Vincenzo Mirco La Fazia, MD,c,d
Giuseppe Stifano, MD,a Chiricolo Gaetano, MD,a,d Andrea Natale, MDc,d,e,f
ABSTRACT
BACKGROUND Painful left bundle branch block (LBBB) syndrome is a rare cause of chest pain associated with
intermittent LBBB.
CASE SUMMARY We report the case of a 68-year-old man who experienced chest pain during a treadmill test.
The temporal relationship between chest pain and the concealed Wenckebach phenomenon in the left bundle branch,
along with the absence of documented myocardial ischemia, strongly suggested a diagnosis of painful LBBB syndrome.
The patient underwent up-titration of a b-blocker.
DISCUSSION The chest pain in painful LBBB syndrome is thought to be related to dyssynchrony in myocardial
contraction caused by intermittent depolarization disturbances. Although rare, the Wenckebach phenomenon can
complicate conduction in the bundle branches, leading to intermittent LBBB. (JACC Case Rep. 2025;30:103751)

HISTORY OF PRESENTATION
A 68-year-old man with a history of hypertension,
dyslipidemia, and chronic coronary syndrome un-
derwent
treadmill
testing
for
interscapular
pain
radiating anteriorly and associated with exertion. The
test was stopped during the second minute of the
second stage of the Bruce protocol due to the begin-
ning of pain that replicated his reported symptoms.
The onset of pain coincided with the onset of
intermittent left bundle branch block (LBBB) on the

electrocardiogram (ECG) (Figure 1). At that
time, his blood pressure was 185/65 mm Hg,

and his heart rate was 136 beats/min. In the
recovery phase, the intermittent LBBB dis-
appeared,
and
the
chest
pain
resolved
simultaneously. Analysis of the narrow QRS
complexes observed after normalization of
intraventricular conduction showed no evi-
dence of myocardial ischemia (Figure 2). The echo-
cardiogram performed at the end of the study showed
no global or segmental wall motion abnormalities.
PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
One month before, the patient had undergone coro-
nary angiography for exertional angina that revealed
an 80% stenosis in the midsegment of the left ante-
rior descending artery, which was treated with an-
gioplasty and drug-eluting stent placement.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
The differential diagnosis included new onset ﬁxed
coronary lesions, early stent failure, coronary spasm,
and painful LBBB syndrome.
INVESTIGATIONS
The patient underwent another coronary angiog-
raphy, which revealed patency of the previously
implanted stent and no new hemodynamically sig-
niﬁcant lesions (Figure 3). An electrophysiological
study was not performed because the patient did not
provide his consent.
MANAGEMENT
The patient underwent medical therapy optimization
with b-blocker up-titration (from 1.25 mg of bisoprolol
to 3.75 mg).
DISCUSSION
The ECG in the Figure 1 (leads V1, V5, and V6 recorded
simultaneously) shows a regular sinus tachycardia.
Most
ventricular
complexes
exhibit
a
LBBB
morphology. However, this pattern normalizes cycli-
cally and reproducibly, with the LBBB disappearing
intermittently.
The normalization of intraventricular conduction
does not depend on variations in the R-R intervals:
cycles ending with narrow complexes are the same as
those ending with wide complexes. A similar behavior
is observed in the PR intervals. Therefore, it can be
concluded that the bundle branch block (BBB) is not
heart rate dependent. The disappearance of the LBBB
occurs in nonpremature beats, thus ruling out su-
pernormal conduction.
The
underlying
mechanism
of
intermittent
conductive
disorder
is
represented
by
concealed

2
Wenckebach phenomenon in the left bundle branch
(LBB), with a predominant 3:2 numerical ratio. The
Wenckebach
phenomenon
involves
a
gradual
lengthening of the conduction time for successive
impulses until one is blocked. The impulse after the
block is conducted better than the one preceding it,
and this cycle repeats.
The
Wenckebach
phenomenon
is
ubiquitous
throughout the conduction tissue and is not conﬁned
to the atrioventricular node.1 Friedberg and Scham-
roth2
were
the
ﬁrst
to
describe
the
concealed
Wenckebach phenomenon in the LBB. The Wenck-
ebach phenomenon in the His-Purkinje system has
recently
been
documented
also
by
endocavitary
electrophysiological studies.3
When the Wenckebach phenomenon complicates
conduction in a bundle branch, 2 types of periodic-
ities can occur.
1. Manifest: characterized by progressive increase in
intraventricular conduction time until complete
BBB occurs.
2. Concealed: can only be deduced from the periodi-
cal, unexpected normalization of intraventricular
conduction, every 2 or more consecutive QRS dis-
playing complete BBB, unrelated to changes in
cycle length.
To
better
understand
the
mechanism
of
BBB
concealment in relation to the ECG presentation, it is
important to consider that the degree of bundle
branch conduction disturbance depends on the con-
duction delay. The smallest delay that allows us to
observe changes in the QRS complex is 0.01 seconds;
a delay between 0.04 and 0.06 seconds results in a
complete BBB.4 It has been hypothesized that such a
delay
allows
the
impulse
to
fully

activate
the
ventricle through the contralateral branch before the
wavefront travels anterogradely through the affected
branch. Further delaying the conduction time in this
branch will not increase the degree of BBB, which will
already be at its maximum.
The ladder diagram (Figure 4) provides a detailed
explanation of the phenomenon. The ﬁrst impulse of

the Wenckebach series is conducted simultaneously
by both branches, producing a narrow QRS. The
second impulse, as expected in a typical Wenck-
ebach sequence, undergoes the maximum delay.
The delay is such that the ventricle is activated
entirely by the impulse conducted over the right
branch, and the resulting QRS displays a pattern of
complete
LBBB.
The
third
impulse
results
in
a
complete conduction failure at the origin of the
LBB.
However,
electrocardiographically,
the
ven-
tricular complex is indistinguishable from the pre-
vious one. After the blocked impulse 3, the LBB has
time enough to recover excitability; consequently,
the next impulse (labeled 4) is conducted simulta-
neously by both bundle branches again, indicating
the presence of concealed Wenckebach phenome-
non indirectly.
Although the most probable diagnosis, considering
the clinical history, is exertional angina, our case
presents elements that call this diagnosis into ques-
tion. The chest pain appears suddenly and coincides
with
the
onset
of
intermittent
LBBB,
and
its
resolution coincides with the disappearance of the
LBBB. After the resolution of chest pain and LBBB, no
signs
suggestive
of
myocardial
ischemia
were
observed in the analysis of the narrow QRS com-
plexes.
Furthermore,
the
coronary
angiography
showed good results from the previously implanted
stent with no new hemodynamically signiﬁcant le-
sions or new onset ﬁxed coronary lesions.
Another explanation for the characteristic elec-
trocardiographic ﬁndings and symptoms is coronary
vasospasm. This condition is often investigated as a
potential cause of unexplained chest pain and is
typically ruled out with ergotamine infusion during
coronary angiography.5-7 In our case, a spontaneous
vasospasm occurred in the proximal segment of
the
left
anterior
descending
artery
during
the
angiography,
which
was
effectively
treated
with
nitroglycerin.
As
a
result,
we
decided
against
administering ergotamine after excluding new-onset
ﬁxed coronary lesions and early stent failure. During
the
vasospasm,
the
patient
did
not
experience
chest
pain,
and
continuous
electrocardiographic

monitoring showed no changes in the duration of
the ventricular depolarization phase consistent with
LBBB.
Therefore,
it
is
highly
unlikely
that
the
vasospasm was related to the clinical presentation
in our case.
The onset and offset of chest pain do not show the
typical
characteristics
of
ischemic
pain,
which
generally begins gradually and increases in intensity
over several minutes. Ischemic pain typically sub-

sides gradually with rest or after taking medications
like nitroglycerin. By contrast, the pain in our pa-
tient’s case did not follow this gradual onset and
resolution pattern, suggesting that it may not have
been related to ischemia.
This pattern, especially the temporal relationship
between chest pain and LBBB, is highly suggestive of
painful LBBB syndrome.8 This is a rare diagnosis of
chest
pain
caused
by
intermittent
LBBB
in
the
absence of myocardial ischemia. Dyssynchrony in
myocardial contraction has been hypothesized as the
main cause of the pain.9,10 As has been previously
described, painful LBBB syndrome can coexist with
coronary artery disease. However, it is often under-
diagnosed in this context.7
FOLLOW-UP
The patient returned for examination 1 month later
and reported no chest pain.
CONCLUSIONS
To the best of our knowledge, we report the ﬁrst case
of painful LBBB syndrome induced by a concealed
Wenckebach phenomenon in the LBB. Painful LBBB is
a rare cause of chest pain and is characterized by the
temporal relationship between chest pain and LBBB.
It requires differential diagnosis that includes ﬁxed
coronary lesions, coronary spasm, and, in our case,
early stent failure. The key criterion for diagnosing
painful LBBB syndrome is not the absence of angio-
graphically documented coronary artery disease but
rather
the
absence
of
objectively
documented
myocardial ischemia.

FIGURE 4
Ladder Diagram of Concealed Wenckebach Phenomenon
The ladder diagram represents the atrium, the atrioventricular junction, the bundle
branches, and the ventricle. It illustrates a concealed Wenckebach sequence in the left
bundle branch (impulses numbered from 1 to 3); the fourth impulse marks the start of a
new sequence. Conduction in the right bundle branch is represented by a solid line, and
conduction in the left bundle branch is depicted by a dashed line. The symbol
illustrates the delayed conduction resulting from the activation of entire ventricular
mass by the contralateral bundle branch. A ¼ atrium; AV ¼ atrioventricular junction;
BB ¼ bundle branches; ECG ¼ electrocardiography; LBB ¼ left bundle branch;
RBB ¼ right bundle branch; V ¼ ventricle.
